1. F36 — ACCEPT closure

Defect

R0.8.6 correctly required the anchor to authorize the exact committed successor, but it authenticated only the endpoint.

A foreign root could remain at the honest anchor's own committed:

revision R
head H0

while carrying:

pending R+1 / Hforeign

produced legitimately under another anchor.

Because the committed root matched the honest anchor:

Root::open
    did not challenge root.pending

Recovery selected roll-forward.

The replay then called the ordinary pending path, whose first act was to write the candidate's pending successor into the honest anchor.

So:

candidate state
    ->
trusted successor authorization

The trust direction was reversed.

This is both:

S3:
    lineage/successor provenance lost during an intermediate transition phase

and an S2-shaped failure:
    recovery evidence minted authority from claimant-provided state

Repair

R0.8.7 introduces two load-bearing protections.

A. The pending state machine is checked at Root::open

For a root with an in-flight transition:

anchor none + root Hx
    REFUSE

anchor H1 + root Hx != H1
    REFUSE

anchor H1 + root H1
    potentially recoverable

The candidate cannot reach recovery while carrying a pending transition this deployment did not already authorize.

B. PendingOrigin

Original
    may CREATE the anchor reservation
    because it originates from this controller's already-verified state

Replay
    must FIND and MATCH an existing reservation
    and can never mint one

The replay/original distinction is derived from the internal recovery path, not from claimant-controlled durable bytes.

Ruling

F36 exact foreign-pending-import defect: CLOSED under the existing R0.8 profile.

Preserve the failing NC29 witness append-only.

Cross-registry interpretation

Do not create a new S-row.

I recommend:

primary:
    S3 continuity / anti-resurrection / successor provenance

cross-reference:
    S2 authority non-amplification

A useful corollary name, if Graphonomous needs one, would be:

S3-PHASE-COMPLETE-PROVENANCE

Every durable intermediate state that can affect recovery must preserve the
same admitted lineage authorization; recovery may complete an admitted
transition but may not manufacture its missing authority from the candidate
being recovered.

This is a corollary / refinement, not a new primitive.

2. F37 — ACCEPT closure

Defect

The F35/F36 ordering intentionally writes:

anchor reservation
BEFORE
root pending transition

so authorization precedes the act.

A real process crash between those two writes reaches:

anchor:
    committed R/H0
    pending   R+1/H1

root:
    committed R/H0
    pending   NONE

store:
    R/H0

R0.8.6 reopened cleanly but left the unused anchor reservation intact.

That reservation could later authorize a candidate that the actual root had never recorded as an in-flight transition.

Repair

R0.8.7 explicitly defines the semantic roles:

anchor.pending
    = RESERVATION / authorization

root.pending
    = durable transition record

Only after Ctl::open has:

opened the root
validated the committed pair
re-derived the semantic history

does reconcile_anchor() cancel:

anchor pending != none
root pending == none
committed anchor == committed root

The controller does not invent a transition or advance the committed lineage.

NC30 reaches this state with an actual crash at:

after-anchor-pending

rather than hand-writing the files.

It then verifies:

reservation existed
root pending did not exist
store did not move

restart succeeds
reservation is cancelled
committed head stays H0

later legitimate transition succeeds

a foreign candidate cannot spend the cancelled slot

Ruling

F37 exact unused-reservation defect: CLOSED under the declared process crash / single-host profile.

This is an S3 lifecycle/currentness refinement, not a new semantic primitive.

4. Requirement e — I recommend one more tiny control before FINAL R0.8 freeze

The remaining question was:

Does the recovery/report surface distinguish "nothing was ever authorized" from "H1 was durably authorized but the root never recorded pending", or is there an explicit design decision that this distinction is intentionally not externally observable?

The current source does not surface this distinction.

In the F37 window:

Ctl::open
    first classifies root/store recovery as clean

later:
    reconcile_anchor()
        mutates the trusted anchor
        cancels the unused reservation

but RecoveryReport.resolution remains:

"clean"

This does not create an S3 safety failure.

After cancellation, the two states are intentionally future-equivalent:

never reserved
reservation existed but was never used and has now been cancelled

So S4 does not require the historical distinction merely because the past bytes differed.

However, R0.8 already treats recovery-report as trusted operator evidence:

  • F20 protects the trusted recovery evidence;

  • F21 keeps recovery-report available under poison while preventing it from

serving contaminated live state;

  • the durable model says ambiguous committed transitions are surfaced rather

than silently guessed.

Given that existing contract, reporting:

resolution = clean

while recovery actually changed the trusted anchor is too ambiguous for a final freeze.

Preferred solution

Add one small control, call it NC31 without minting a new F-number yet.

Reach the real F37 crash window and assert the restart reports something like:

resolution:
    "unused-anchor-reservation-cancelled"

or fields:

anchor_reservation_recovered = true
cancelled_successor_revision = R+1
cancelled_successor_head = H1

The report need not make the reservation a semantic World transition.

It is diagnostic recovery evidence about trusted infrastructure.

Alternative

If the architecture deliberately defines:

recovery-report.resolution
    = semantic root/store transition recovery only

and explicitly excludes internal currentness-reservation cleanup, document that contract and add a control proving "clean" means exactly that.

I prefer surfacing the cancellation.

Ruling

Do not mint F38 merely from this review.

First make the contract explicit and let NC31 determine whether current behavior violates it.

10. L1 three-assumption contract — enable is the right current granularity

The v2.7 finite temporal model now separates:

ENV-SUCCESSOR-AVAILABILITY
    a willing/eligible candidate is offered

SYS-SUCCESSOR-ENABLEMENT
    the system turns a valid offer into an admissible successor opportunity

SYS-ATTACH-FAIRNESS
    a continuously enabled admissible attachment is eventually processed

and shows omission of enablement breaks service succession.

That is a useful result.

Should enablement be split into authority / policy / finality proof now?

No, not yet.

At the current semantic level:

SYS-SUCCESSOR-ENABLEMENT

is the right obligation.

Authority, policy, generation/finality proof, resource compatibility and world/locus admission are candidate mechanisms / preconditions that discharge enablement.

Do not turn every conjunction inside a mechanism into another liveness law.

Split enablement only if we can construct an independence witness such as:

authority available, policy unavailable -> liveness fails in a distinct way
policy available, finality proof unavailable -> ...

and the distinctions matter semantically rather than operationally.

For Graphonomous, represent:

L1
    REQUIRES -> SYS-SUCCESSOR-ENABLEMENT

SYS-SUCCESSOR-ENABLEMENT
    DISCHARGED_BY -> authority evidence
    DISCHARGED_BY -> policy admission
    DISCHARGED_BY -> finality/generation proof
    DISCHARGED_BY -> resource compatibility

until reduction/falsification shows those deserve separate obligations.

11. E-51 — claim-time SATISFIED-REPEAT line needs one further refinement

The v2.7 model's basic distinction is correct:

UNKNOWN:
    ordinary replay refused
    REPLAY_RISK_AUTHORIZED may admit a replay

SATISFIED:
    same intent is done
    another physical effect is a NEW intent

FAILED-ABSENT:
    retry under the same intent may be admissible

I accept that.

But I do not think claim-time classification alone is sufficient.

Consider:

t0:
    intent K is UNKNOWN

t1:
    operator grants REPLAY_RISK_AUTHORIZED

t2:
    replay attempt A2 is CLAIMED

t3:
    before A2 crosses the irreversible effect boundary,
    reconciliation establishes that A1 actually COMMITTED

t4:
    A2 performs the external effect anyway

At t2, the replay was legitimately admitted under uncertainty.

At t3, uncertainty is gone.

If A2 has not yet crossed the irreversible effect boundary, continuing at t4 creates a duplicate that was no longer necessary and is avoidable using information the system already has.

Therefore add:

EFFECT-TIME CURRENTNESS / REVALIDATION

A replay-risk authorization permits an attempt while completion is UNKNOWN,
but immediately before the irreversible effect boundary the attempt must
revalidate the intent's current satisfaction state.

if still UNKNOWN:
    proceed under REPLAY_RISK_AUTHORIZED

if SATISFIED before effect:
    do not effect
    terminate/supersede/cancel the replay attempt

if the replay already crossed the effect boundary while UNKNOWN and the
original is only later discovered COMMITTED:
    any resulting duplicate is an ACKNOWLEDGED-RISK duplicate

This is the same architectural pattern we have seen elsewhere:

authority/admission at proposal time
!=
authority/currentness at use time

Do not mint a new E-number from prose alone.

Extend the finite model first.

Answer to the v5 question

So:

an authorized replay claimed while UNKNOWN whose duplicate lands after the original is reconciled COMMITTED is an acknowledged duplicate only if the replay had already crossed the irreversible effect boundary before that resolution became available, or if the boundary could not safely observe the new information.

If satisfaction becomes known while the replay is still safely cancellable, the effect boundary should refuse it.

That is the sharper line.

16. Final ruling

v5 is a successful execution return precisely because NC29 did not merely go green.

It exposed that endpoint provenance was insufficient:

OURS AT COMMIT
!=
OURS THROUGHOUT THE TRANSITION

and then exposed that an authorization itself has a lifecycle:

AUTHORIZED
but never used
must not remain spendable forever

R0.8.7 repairs both exact defects coherently.

The resulting semantic picture is cleaner:

anchor reservation
    authorizes a specific successor

root pending
    proves the transition actually entered the durable recovery protocol

replay
    may complete an existing authorization
    never create one

unused reservation
    is cancelled after verified recovery

committed successor
    must be the exact authorized head

That looks like a total phase model of S3 successor provenance, not another new primitive.

The one thing I would still resolve before the final R0.8 freeze is whether a trusted-anchor cancellation during recovery is visible in the trusted recovery-report.

After that, if no new process-crash defect appears:

freeze R0.8 within its declared profile and move on.

No broad Fable invariant-search round is warranted.
